title: ReviewDebt: a practical framework for scoring every pull request — Sachin Gupta, Ebay

primary.label: Coding Agents & Software Engineering
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 88%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary object is AI coding agents in the PR review loop and the hidden review burden they create, directly matching the inclusion criterion for code review as the main research object. Coding assistants covers the Copilot, Cursor, and Codex context; developer_platforms is its parent domain; enterprise_operations covers engineering team workflows and the governance outlook. The framework is validated on 524 PRs across three repos, deployed via five adoption steps, includes weekly dashboard monitoring, and projects 2027 governance needs. Requires familiarity with PR review workflows, CI/CD pipelines, and basic coding-agent concepts, but the framework itself is explained accessibly for practicing engineers. Conference presentation from the AI Engineer channel with CLI walkthrough and 90-day dashboard demonstrations. All claims are stated directly in the transcript with specific quantitative data and cited industry reports from GitHub, Faros AI, and DX.

summary: Sachin Gupta opens by framing the core problem: coding agents produce code faster than humans can responsibly review it, creating an unmeasured debt he calls review debt. He cites GitHub's October 2025 report showing commits up 25% year-over-year while review comments dropped 27%, and Faros AI's 2026 benchmark showing median PR review time up 441.5%, reviewed PRs taking 5.4 times longer, and 31% more PRs merged with no review. DX 2026 study data shows PRs per developer up 16%, median PR size up 63% from 44 to 72 lines, and AI usage up 65%, yet he argues these are vanity metrics that measure production speed, not trust speed. He defines review debt as the accumulating gap between code agents produce and code humans have reviewed, trusted, and understood. It compounds through three feedback loops: agents learning from unreviewed code, reviewers contracting to syntax-level checks while architecture drifts, and leadership resetting velocity expectations without reviewer capacity. Gupta introduces five signal families with 10 deterministic checks—diff size and coupling, test evidence gap, directory and ownership spread, AI authorship indicators, and evidence and rationale gaps—deliberately avoiding LLM-as-judge for defensibility. He then demonstrates the CLI scanner on three real PRs: a clean human PR scoring 0 with 6 estimated minutes, a high-debt PR scoring 60 with 86 minutes and structured advice lists, and a well-shaped AI-authored PR scoring 7 with 14 minutes. The AI authorship indicator is explicitly framed as information only, not a penalty; it contributes only 5 of 60 points on the high-debt PR. He presents 90-day dashboard data across 524 PRs in three public repos showing review burden climbs with PR volume even when AI authorship share stays flat at 5–20%. Across 524 PRs the scanner estimated 228 cumulative senior reviewer hours, one repo accumulated 186 hours in 27 days, and a single PR required an estimated 84 hours of review effort scoring 73. Only four PRs landed in needs-evidence or high bands, all structural changes. He concludes with five adoption steps—backfill, threshold, surface, aggregate, talk about it—and practical engineering habits: one logical change per PR, tests ship with change, stay in one owner territory, author writes the why, and same review standards for AI and human PRs.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: Review debt is the compounding gap between code agents produce and code humans have actually reviewed, trusted, and understood, analogous to financial debt where interest is paid in human attention.
Traditional metrics—PR count, cycle time, lines of code—are vanity metrics that measure production speed, not trust speed.
The framework uses five signal families with 10 deterministic checks, deliberately avoiding LLM-as-judge so scores remain stable and defensible in engineering reviews.

Volume drives review debt, not AI authorship: across 524 PRs, AI authorship was flat at 5–20% but review burden varied wildly by PR volume, with one repo accumulating 186 senior reviewer hours in 27 days.
The AI authorship indicator is information only, not a penalty; it contributes minimally to scores and fires only when other signals are weak.
The structured advice output—reviewer focus list and author next-action list—is what moves team behavior, not the score alone.

Five adoption steps: backfill over last 200 merged PRs, set a justify threshold (default 50), surface scores as non-blocking PR comments, aggregate weekly per team, and bring the number to retrospectives.

Practical habits reduce debt: one logical change per PR, tests ship with change asserting intended behavior, stay in one owner territory, human author writes the PR rationale, and same review standards for AI and human PRs.
Plotting the weekly slope of review debt matters more than the absolute level; the slope is the leading indicator engineering managers should watch.
2027 will shift the conversation to governance—accountability, audit trails, and trust boundaries—where ReviewDebt bridges velocity gains and governance needs.

sections.title: Introduction and the Gap Nobody Is Measuring
sections.summary: Sachin Gupta introduces the talk, clarifying that coding agents are not bad and do make us faster, but they create an unmeasured debt. He cites GitHub's October 2025 report showing commits up 25% year-over-year while review comments dropped 27%, and Faros AI's 2026 benchmark showing median PR review time up 441.5%, reviewed PRs taking 5.4 times longer, and 31% more PRs merged with no review.

sections.title: Vanity Metrics and the Real Story
sections.summary: Gupta presents DX 2026 study data showing PRs per developer up 16%, median PR size up 63% from 44 to 72 lines, cycle time modestly down, throughput up 8%, and AI usage up 65%. He argues these are all vanity metrics measuring production speed, not trust speed. He then describes reviewer fatigue, late-night merges, test theater, architectural drift, and incident lag as hidden costs no dashboard captures.

sections.title: Definition of Review Debt and Compounding Loops
sections.summary: Review debt is defined as the accumulating gap between code agents produce and code humans have reviewed, trusted, and understood. It compounds like financial debt with interest paid in human attention. Three feedback loops drive compounding: agents learning from unreviewed code, reviewers contracting to syntax-level checks while architectural decisions slip, and leadership resetting velocity expectations without proportional reviewer capacity.

sections.title: Five Signal Families Overview
sections.summary: Gupta introduces five signal families with 10 deterministic checks: diff size and coupling, test evidence gap, directory and ownership spread, AI authorship indicators, and evidence and rationale gaps. He deliberately avoids LLM-as-judge because scores become moving targets when models change and lose defensibility in engineering reviews.

sections.title: Signal 1: Diff Size and Coupling
sections.summary: Diff size and coupling measures net lines changed, files touched, and whether changes cluster in one module or sprawl across many. Agents are biased toward fixing at call sites across many files, while humans route fixes to root causes keeping diffs small. Sprawling diffs exponentially increase the mental model reviewers must hold.

sections.title: Signal 2: Test Evidence Gap
sections.summary: Test evidence gap is test lines added divided by production lines added per PR. AI-authored PRs ship with far lower test-to-code ratios, and when tests exist they often assert what code does rather than what it should do, locking in bugs. The ratio only measures whether tests showed up, not their quality.

sections.title: Signal 3: Directory and Ownership Spread
sections.summary: Directory and ownership spread counts distinct code-owner teams whose files appear in the diff. Well-shaped PRs concentrate in one team directory; sprawling PRs require multiple approvals from multiple engineers in different contexts. The coordination overhead easily exceeds the time the agent saved producing code, making the economics of review debt tangible.

sections.title: Signal 4: AI Authorship Indicators
sections.summary: AI authorship indicators detect agent-assisted PRs through three signals: co-authored footers (strongest), branch name patterns with prefixes like codex, Copilot, cursor, and generated-by or assisted-by phrases in PR bodies or commit messages. Real data from 524 PRs across three repos confirmed co-authored footer as the highest signal, while repo C showed 0% signal despite agent usage.

sections.title: Signal 5: Evidence and Rationale Gaps
sections.summary: Evidence and rationale gaps measure whether a PR explains why, not just what. A high-gap example had an 18-character body and commit message saying updates. A low-gap example included symptom, diagnosis, change description, and benchmark link. This signal destroys reviewability fastest, though it fires rarely in open source repos following conventional commit format.

sections.title: Scoring System and Calibration
sections.summary: The five signals combine into a single 0-100 score with default weights. Gupta recommends calibrating by running the scanner backwards over the last 200 merged PRs and tuning weights against actual reviewer experience. Four bands map to actions: 0-24 low burden, 25-49 normal, 50-74 needs author evidence before senior review, 75+ high split or request more context.

sections.title: CLI Walkthrough: Three Scored PRs Side by Side
sections.summary: Gupta demonstrates the scanner on three PRs. A clean human PR scores 0/100 with 6 estimated minutes and no checks fired, producing a tiny ceremonial report. A high-debt PR scores 60/100 with 86 estimated minutes, generating a structured wire list, reviewer focus list, and author next-action list. The AI indicator contributed only 5 of 60 points, and the output explicitly states it is information only, not a penalty. A well-shaped AI-authored PR scores 7/100 with 14 minutes because tests were added, CI was green, and risky paths were called out. The AI indicator contributed 2.1 of 7 points at low severity, again labeled information only.

sections.title: 90-Day Dashboard: 524 PRs Across Three Public Repos
sections.summary: Gupta presents a 90-day AI share slope across three public repos and 524 PRs. Three observations emerge: volume is the actual variable driving burden while AI authorship stayed flat at 5–20%; the positioning contract holds under real data with no AI-authored PRs disproportionately landing in high-burden bands; and complexity drives burden, not authorship, with only four PRs in needs-evidence or high bands—all structural changes like large migrations, SDK rewrites, and multi-team refactors. In absolute terms the scanner saw 228 cumulative senior reviewer hours, one repo accumulated 186 hours in 27 days, the high-velocity repo sustained 9 PRs per day, and a single PR required an estimated 84 hours of review effort scoring 73.

sections.title: Practical Habits to Reduce Review Debt
sections.summary: Gupta lists five engineering habits: one logical change per PR, tests ship with the change with human confirmation that tests assert intended behavior, stay in one owner territory with cross-cutting work split per team, the human author writes the PR rationale rather than the agent, and the same review standards apply to AI and human PRs. The AI indicator amplifier only fires when other signals are weak, so keeping the other four strong makes it invisible. None of these require a new tool.

sections.title: Five Adoption Steps and Governance Outlook
sections.summary: Gupta outlines five adoption steps: backfill by running the scorer over the last 200 merged PRs, set a justify threshold (default 50 requiring author comment), surface scores as non-blocking PR comments, aggregate weekly per team where the slope is the leading indicator, and talk about the number in retrospectives and roadmap reviews. He argues the number moves discussions from feeling to measurement. Looking to 2027, he predicts a governance shift around accountability and audit trails for AI-authored changes, with ReviewDebt bridging velocity gains and governance needs. Three final takeaways: measure the gap with 20 PRs from last week, make the weekly slope visible, and bring the number to reviews. He closes with anti-patterns to avoid: approve-with-comment merges, deferring to QA, assuming smaller PRs are fine, and writing LGTM.

evidence.excerpt: Your coding agent is creating review debt. Before I start, sit with the title for a second. Notice what it is not saying. I'm not saying that coding agents are bad.
evidence.supports: Review debt is the core thesis, not an anti-AI argument

evidence.excerpt: GitHub's 2025 October's report that covers almost every public pull request on the planet shows that the commits climbed 25% year over year. And now over the same year, comments on the comments dropped 27%.
evidence.supports: Code production volume increased while review attention decreased

evidence.excerpt: It's the accumulating gap between code your agent has produced and the code humans have actually reviewed, trusted, and understood. It rhymes with technical debt, but it is more like a financial debt because it compounds.
evidence.supports: Formal definition of review debt and its compounding nature

evidence.excerpt: the keyword here is deterministic. Every check is computable from a pull request and its repository. No, we don't need any language model.
evidence.supports: Framework deliberately avoids LLM-as-judge for deterministic, defensible scoring

evidence.excerpt: Run it backwards over the last 200 PRs that have been merged in your company. Calibrate the weights against your team's actual reviewer experience. The score has to feel right against your actual guts.
evidence.supports: Teams must calibrate scoring weights against their own historical PRs and reviewer experience

evidence.excerpt: PR has soft indicators of AI assisted authorship. This is information only, not a definitive claim, and not a penalty on its own.
evidence.supports: AI authorship indicator is explicitly information-only, not a penalty

evidence.excerpt: volume is the actual variable. AI authorship was flat and it was 5 to 20% steady state, but the review burden was not.
evidence.supports: PR volume, not AI authorship, drives review burden accumulation

evidence.excerpt: 5,036. These are the minutes that are basically spent on a single PR, which is nothing but 84 hours of review effort estimated for one single pull request.
evidence.supports: Single highest-burden PR required estimated 84 hours of review effort

evidence.excerpt: Backfill. So, you run the scorer over your last 200 merge PR. Look at the one basically that has the highest score. Second, threshold. Set a basically justify line. Default, let's say you want to give it 50.
evidence.supports: Five-step adoption begins with backfill over last 200 PRs and setting a justify threshold at 50

evidence.excerpt: Take 20 PRs from the last week, score them using the five signals that we discussed. You will basically get a number so that you will understand, okay, whether the framework is working right or not.
evidence.supports: Immediate next step is scoring 20 PRs from last week to validate the framework
